backTranslations.41:
**Before the visit**
- On the Visit tab add the date of the visit. MenoMap shows how ready your notes are and what would still improve them.
- Choose the topics and questions that matter most to you. Three or four is enough.
- Create notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**At the visit**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is designed to be readable in under a minute: counts, averages, a heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What the notes are and are not**

They are a summary of what you entered and of anything you chose to bring over from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis or a complete medical record, and any patterns in them are a coincidence check, not proof of cause. The doctor may ask about things the notes will not answer, and that is normal.

**After the visit**

Add each new medication with the date you started taking it. In a few weeks MenoMap can show you your records before and after, which makes the next check-up easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single moment: the day when 12 months in a row without a period have passed, unless something else explains it (for example pregnancy, certain medications or surgery). In many countries it occurs on average in the early fifties, but anything from the mid-forties to the mid-fifties is common.

**Perimenopause** is the period of years that precedes this moment. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can be irregular, heavier, lighter, more frequent or less frequent. Many changes people associate with the change, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, often begin already here, while periods still come. Perimenopause can last several years or significantly longer and it goes differently for everyone.

**Postmenopause** is everything after this twelve-month boundary. Some troubles fade over time, others can last for years.

Menopause can also happen earlier, because of surgery in which the ovaries are removed, some cancer treatments or other health conditions. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency and it is worth discussing with a doctor.

**How it is recognized.** For many people over 45, a doctor recognizes perimenopause or menopause from your health history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always needed, because hormone levels fluctuate from day to day. They are used rather when someone is younger or when the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap can and cannot do.** MenoMap cannot tell you what stage you are in. But it can honestly record what you notice: waves, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your doctor can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden feeling of heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with redness, sweating, a pounding heart or a feeling of cold afterwards. A night sweat is the same during sleep and can be so strong that it wakes you or soaks the bedding.

They are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people have only a few mild ones; others have many a day and they disrupt their work and sleep. In some they fade within a few years; in others they last much longer.

**What can trigger them more often.** People often notice a connection with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress or a heavy blanket. It varies a lot from person to person, which is why tracking your own tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There are other causes too.** Flushing and sweating can also be caused by thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not match the usual course or are accompanied by weight loss, fever or a general feeling of being ill, tell your doctor.

**How to describe them well.** Useful information for the visit:
- About how many you have per day and per night
- How strong they are and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What seems to precede them
- What you have tried and whether it changed anything

The Wave button and the look-back entry in MenoMap are there precisely so you can capture this without much effort.

**Help exists.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options and also practical approaches. Which of them suits you is a topic for a conversation with your doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces part of the estrogen that the body makes less of around menopause. Leading professional guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats in many people and it can help with other symptoms too.

**It comes in various forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets and low-dose vaginal products for local problems such as dryness. Those who still have a uterus are usually prescribed a progestogen together with estrogen, which protects the lining of the uterus.

**Benefits and risks depend on the individual:** on age, on how long you have been without a period, on your personal and family health history (for example breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease) and on the type and way of administering the treatment. That is why it is a decision made with a doctor who knows your history, not something an app can decide.

**What people often ask:**
- Is hormone therapy a suitable option for me? Why or why not?
- What type and what form do you recommend to me and why?
- What benefits can I expect and how soon?
- What are my personal risks and how do they compare with not being treated?
- What should I watch for and when will we review this again together?

**If you already take it,** enter it in MenoMap (Me → Medications). MenoMap shows your waves before starting treatment and after, as a coincidence check, not proof, so that you have something concrete to talk about at the review.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not suitable for everyone and some people simply prefer other paths. There are several.

**Prescription medications.** For some non-hormonal medications there is evidence that they ease hot flashes. They include some medications originally developed for other conditions and a newer class of medications developed directly for hot flashes. Each has its benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talk therapy and mind-body approaches.** For cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause there is evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes that help people:**
- Layers of clothing you can quickly take off
- A fan at the work desk and at the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Noticing personal triggers and easing them (tags and experiments in MenoMap help here)
- Regular movement and a steady sleep routine

**Dietary supplements and herbal products.** For many of them the evidence is unclear or limited, their quality varies and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take, including over-the-counter products.

**Try one change at a time.** Two-week experiments in MenoMap compare your own records before the change and during it, which is easier to judge than a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most doctor visits are short and recalling a month of nights on the spot is hard. People usually remember the last days or the worst ones. A simple record fills that gap.

**What a diary gives your doctor:**
- How often symptoms come and how strong they are, not just that they come
- Whether things are improving, worsening or staying the same
- What was going on around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A starting point for comparison if you try some treatment

**Don't let it be a burden.** A diary helps only if you keep it. MenoMap is built on the one-tap Wave button and an evening entry with four questions, so it takes seconds, not a whole notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of records usually show a clearer picture than one bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. The Visit tab in MenoMap helps you choose questions and prints them together with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
Once 12 months without a period have passed, **any vaginal bleeding should be checked by a doctor**, even if it appears only once, and even if it is only spotting or a light pink or brown discharge.

Mostly it turns out the cause is not serious. For example, thinning of the lining of the vagina or uterus is common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat when caught early. That is why public health guidance advises having it examined and not waiting.

**If you take hormone therapy,** a certain pattern of bleeding can be expected depending on its type. Bleeding that is not expected with your treatment, is heavier than usual or comes at the wrong time should also be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your doctor or healthcare facility and say that you had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, the amount and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can keep this for you (Me → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding happened. It reminds you to have it checked and includes it in the notes for the visit.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is one of the most common troubles in middle age and rarely has a single cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly, or afterwards you may be so hot or damp that you do not fall asleep again.

**Other common influences:**
- Needing to urinate at night
- Anxiety or a restless mind
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but rather fragments the second half of the night
- Caffeine later in the day
- Pain, restless legs or a partner's snoring
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be a sign of sleep apnea (worth mentioning, especially if you are very sleepy during the day)

**What usually helps people.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layers of clothing you can throw off; a regular wake-up time; and less alcohol before bed. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied approach and many doctors can recommend a route to it for you.

**What to track.** For a week or two write down your sleep score, night waves, alcohol and late caffeine. The evening entry and wave logging in MenoMap manage this in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show you sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside night sweats, as context, not as an explanation.

**When to get checked.** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (for example while driving), your mood or daily life, or if you notice that you stop breathing or gasp for breath at night.
